raw_case_text: A 68-year-old male patient with a background history of hypertension presented with abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant associated with anorexia for 1-month duration. However, he did not report any fever, chills, altered bowel habits, melena, or per rectal bleeding. He had no previous abdominal surgeries. The general examination was unremarkable, devoid of any fever or tachycardia but the abdominal examination revealed a palpable liver extending beyond the costal margin. His basic blood biochemistry revealed an elevated leucocyte count of 16.8 x 103/microL with a C-reactive protein level of 9.4 mg/L and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 119 mm/h. His liver and renal profiles were normal. Ultrasound abdomen revealed a hypoechoic lesion in the liver measuring 8.9 x 6.4 cm involving liver segments V, VI, and VII without internal vascularity suggestive of a liver abscess. Further imaging with triphasic CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a large irregular shaped loculated peripheral enhancing, centrally hypo-attenuated fluid density lesion measuring 8.3 x 10.8 x 6.1 cm in size involving segment IVA and IVB of the liver suggestive of a liver abscess with mass effect on the common hepatic artery branches (Figure 1). The CT did not show any features of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary obstruction. The collection was drained under ultrasound guidance with a pigtail catheter. Aspirated purulent fluid investigations confirmed a liver abscess. The full report revealed 17,600 mm3 of pus cells and protein of 9000 mg/dL with a significant growth of Escherichia coli, suggestive of the diagnosis of a liver abscess with cytology report confirming the diagnosis. The mycobacterial investigations for tuberculosis, amoebiasis, and Burkholderia pseudomallei, three important causes for liver abscess in South Asian region were negative. Upon further investigations, an elevated HbA1c of 6.4% in the pre-diabetic range was found although FBS was normal. Echocardiography was normal without any features to suggest endocarditis. The investigation for a cause continued with upper GI endoscopy, which was normal. However, interestingly, the colonoscopy revealed a denture impacted at the sigmoid colon adjacent to multiple diverticula. There was no endoscopic feature of diverticulitis. The patient was unaware of having swallowed a denture. The denture was removed carefully using a snare and foreign body forceps. There was superficial ulceration at the site of impaction but no obvious perforation seen on careful examination. It was thought that a microperforation would have spontaneously healed during the delayed personation. The patient was treated with intravenous cefotaxime for 2 weeks according to the sensitivity reports. The patients had an uneventful recovery. He discharged following 2-week hospital stay. Serial follow-up ultrasound scans revealed a resolving abscess. As the denture had only plastic attachments, it was difficult to identify on the previous CT scans; however, there was evidence of colonic perforation from a foreign body depicted in the CECT images retrospectively (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain and anorexia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by anorexia for 1 month prior to presentation. He was unaware of having previously swallowed a plastic-attachment denture.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of hypertension; no prior abdominal surgeries; subsequently found to have pre-diabetes (HbA1c 6.4%).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right upper quadrant abdominal pain and anorexia. Negative for fever, chills, altered bowel habits, melena, or hematochezia.

objective.physical_examination: General examination was unremarkable without fever or tachycardia. Abdominal examination revealed tender/palpable hepatomegaly extending below the right costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Leukocyte count was elevated at 16.8 x 10^3/microL, CRP was 9.4 mg/L, and ESR was 119 mm/h. Liver and renal function profiles and fasting blood sugar were normal, while HbA1c was 6.4%. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed an avascular hypoechoic liver lesion measuring 8.9 x 6.4 cm involving segments V, VI, and VII.
objective.advanced_workup: Triphasic contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a large, irregular, loculated, peripherally enhancing, centrally hypoattenuating liver abscess measuring 8.3 x 10.8 x 6.1 cm in segments IVA and IVB with mass effect on the common hepatic artery branches and no biliary obstruction (retrospective CT review also showed evidence of foreign-body colonic perforation). Ultrasound-guided pigtail catheter aspiration yielded purulent fluid with 17,600/mm^3 pus cells and protein of 9,000 mg/dL; microbiological studies for tuberculosis, amebiasis, and Burkholderia pseudomallei were negative. Upper GI endoscopy was normal, whereas colonoscopy identified an impacted plastic denture in the sigmoid colon adjacent to multiple diverticula with superficial mucosal ulceration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pyogenic Escherichia coli liver abscess secondary to occult sigmoid colon impaction and microperforation by an ingested denture, confirmed by purulent aspirate culture growing E. coli and colonoscopic visualization/retrieval of the impacted sigmoid denture (tuberculosis, amebiasis, and melioidosis were excluded). Management and clinical course: Treated with ultrasound-guided percutaneous pigtail catheter drainage, endoscopic removal of the impacted sigmoid denture using a snare and foreign-body forceps, and a 2-week course of susceptibility-guided intravenous cefotaxime. He made an uneventful recovery, was discharged after 2 weeks, and demonstrated progressive abscess resolution on serial follow-up ultrasounds.
